'''''Mangifera''''' is a [[genus]] of [[flowering plant]]s in the family [[Anacardiaceae]]. It contains 64 species, with the best-known being the common [[mango]] (''[[Mangifera indica]]''). The [[center of diversity]] of the genus is in the [[Malesia]]n ecoregion of [[Southeast Asia]], particularly in [[Sumatra]], [[Borneo]], and the [[Malay Peninsula]].<ref name="Kuhn">{{cite journal |last1=Kuhn |first1=David N. |last2=Dillon |first2=Natalie |last3=Bally |first3=Ian |last4=Groh |first4=Amy |last5=Rahaman |first5=Jordon |last6=Warschefsky |first6=Emily |last7=Freeman |first7=Barbie |last8=Innes |first8=David |last9=Chambers |first9=Alan H. |title=Estimation of genetic diversity and relatedness in a mango germplasm collection using SNP markers and a simplified visual analysis method |journal=Scientia Horticulturae |date=June 2019 |volume=252 |pages=156–168 |doi=10.1016/j.scienta.2019.03.037|s2cid=132739368 |doi-access=free |bibcode=2019ScHor.252..156K }}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=Mangifera indica |url=https://www.cabi.org/isc/datasheet/34505#tosummaryOfInvasiveness |website=Invasive Species Compendium |publisher=CABI |access-date=7 December 2019}}</ref> They are generally [[Canopy (forest)|canopy]] [[tree]]s in lowland [[Tropical and subtropical moist broadleaf forests|rainforests]], reaching a height of {{convert|30|-|40|m|ft|abbr=on}}.<ref name="Litz1">{{cite encyclopedia |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=AxbUJntXepEC |title=''Mangifera indica'' Mango |first=Richard E. |last=Litz |author2=Miguel A. Gómez-Lim |editor=Richard E. Litz |encyclopedia=Biotechnology of Fruit and Nut Crops |year=2005 |publisher=CABI |isbn=978-0-85199-662-2 |pages=40–41}}</ref>

==Uses==
''Mangifera'' species are widely cultivated in Asia and elsewhere. More than 27 species in the genus bear edible, fleshy [[fruit]]s, especially the common mango (''M. indica''). Others, such as ''[[Mangifera foetida|M. foetida]]'', yield astringent fruits that can be eaten [[Pickling|pickled]].<ref>{{cite book |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=oloEhPYqE8QC |title=The Mango: Botany, Production and Uses |edition=2nd |first=Richard E. |last=Litz |year=2009 |publisher=CABI |isbn=978-1-84593-489-7 |pages=5–8}}</ref> Mango residue, such as the seed kernel and peel, have functional and nutritional potential.<ref>{{cite journal | doi=10.1016/j.tifs.2016.06.009| title=Mango seed: Functional and nutritional properties|journal=Trends in Food Science & Technology| volume=55| pages=109–117| year=2016| last1=Torres-León| first1=Cristian| last2=Rojas| first2=Romeo| last3=Serna| first3=Liliana| last4=Contreras| first4=Juan| last5=Aguilar| first5=Cristobal| s2cid=89179753}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal | doi=10.1080/87559129.2015.1094815| title=Agro-industrial potential of the mango peel based on its nutritional and functional properties|journal=Food Reviews International| volume=32| pages=364–376| year=2016| last1=Serna| first1=Liliana| last2=García-Gonzales| first2=Estefanía| last3=Torres-León| first3=Cristian| issue=4| s2cid=87396909}}</ref>

==Uses==
''Mangifera'' species are widely cultivated in Asia and elsewhere. More than 27 species in the genus bear edible, fleshy [[fruit]]s, especially the common mango (''M. indica''). Others, such as ''[[Mangifera foetida|M. foetida]]'', yield astringent fruits that can be eaten [[Pickling|pickled]].<ref>{{cite book |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=oloEhPYqE8QC |title=The Mango: Botany, Production and Uses |edition=2nd |first=Richard E. |last=Litz |year=2009 |publisher=CABI |isbn=978-1-84593-489-7 |pages=5–8}}</ref>

Mango wastes, such as the seed kernel and peel, have high functional and nutritional potential. Mango seed contains important bioactive compounds that have high [[antioxidant]] activity, lipids that have acceptable physical and chemical characteristics (free of ''trans'' fatty acids), and a somewhat high (about 6%) [[protein]] content.<ref>{{cite journal | doi=10.1016/j.tifs.2016.06.009| title=Mango seed: Functional and nutritional properties|journal=Trends in Food Science & Technology| volume=55| pages=109–117| year=2016| last1=Torres-León| first1=Cristian| last2=Rojas| first2=Romeo| last3=Serna| first3=Liliana| last4=Contreras| first4=Juan| last5=Aguilar| first5=Cristobal| s2cid=89179753}}</ref> The mango peel contains considerable amounts of [[antioxidants]] and [[dietary fiber]].<ref>{{cite journal | doi=10.1080/87559129.2015.1094815| title=Agro-industrial potential of the mango peel based on its nutritional and functional properties|journal=Food Reviews International| volume=32| pages=364–376| year=2016| last1=Serna| first1=Liliana| last2=García-Gonzales| first2=Estefanía| last3=Torres-León| first3=Cristian| issue=4| s2cid=87396909}}</ref>

==Fossil record==
The earliest [[fossil]] species thought to be related to ''Mangifera'' is ''[[Eomangiferophyllum damalgiriense]]'' from the upper [[Paleocene]] in northeastern [[India]]. Leaves have also been reported from the Paleocene of [[Japan]] and the [[Eocene]] of [[Germany]], though these have been considered questionable. Leaf fossils confidently assignable to ''Mangifera'' have been collected from [[Oligocene]] or early [[Miocene]] sediments in northern [[Thailand]].<ref>{{Cite journal |author=Prakart Sawangchote |author2=Paul J. The [[center of diversity]] of the genus is in the [[Malesia]]n ecoregion of [[Southeast Asia]], particularly in [[Sumatra]], [[Borneo]], and the [[Malay Peninsula]].<ref name="Kuhn">{{cite journal |last1=Kuhn |first1=David N. |last2=Dillon |first2=Natalie |last3=Bally |first3=Ian |last4=Groh |first4=Amy |last5=Rahaman |first5=Jordon |last6=Warschefsky |first6=Emily |last7=Freeman |first7=Barbie |last8=Innes |first8=David |last9=Chambers |first9=Alan H. |title=Estimation of genetic diversity and relatedness in a mango germplasm collection using SNP markers and a simplified visual analysis method |journal=Scientia Horticulturae |date=June 2019 |volume=252 |pages=156–168 |doi=10.1016/j.scienta.2019.03.037|s2cid=132739368 |doi-access=free |bibcode=2019ScHor.252..156K }}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=Mangifera indica |url=https://www.cabi.org/isc/datasheet/34505#tosummaryOfInvasiveness |website=Invasive Species Compendium |publisher=CABI |access-date=7 December 2019}}</ref> They are generally [[Canopy (forest)|canopy]] [[tree]]s in lowland [[Tropical and subtropical moist broadleaf forests|rainforests]], reaching a height of {{convert|30|-|40|m|ft|abbr=on}}.<ref name="Litz1">{{cite encyclopedia |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=AxbUJntXepEC |title=''Mangifera indica'' Mango |first=Richard E. |last=Litz |author2=Miguel A. Gómez-Lim |editor=Richard E. Litz |encyclopedia=Biotechnology of Fruit and Nut Crops |year=2005 |publisher=CABI |isbn=978-0-85199-662-2 |pages=40–41}}</ref>

==Uses==
''Mangifera'' species are widely cultivated in Asia and elsewhere. More than 27 species in the genus bear edible, fleshy [[fruit]]s, especially the common mango (''M. indica''). Others, such as ''[[Mangifera foetida|M. foetida]]'', yield astringent fruits that can be eaten [[Pickling|pickled]].<ref>{{cite book |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=oloEhPYqE8QC |title=The Mango: Botany, Production and Uses |edition=2nd |first=Richard E. |last=Litz |year=2009 |publisher=CABI |isbn=978-1-84593-489-7 |pages=5–8}}</ref>

Mango wastes, such as the seed kernel and peel, have high functional and nutritional potential. Mango seed contains important bioactive compounds that have high [[antioxidant]] activity, lipids that have acceptable physical and chemical characteristics (free of ''trans'' fa nutritional properties|journal=Trends in Food Science & Technology| volume=55| pages=109–117| year=2016| last1=Torres-León| first1=Cristian| last2=Rojas| first2=Romeo| last3=Serna| first3=Liliana| last4=Contreras| first4=Juan| last5=Aguilar| first5=Cristobal| s2cid=89179753}}</ref> The mango peel contains considerable amounts of [[antioxidants]] and [[dietary fiber]].<ref>{{cite journal | doi=10.1080/87559129.2015.1094815| title=Agro-industrial potential of the mango peel based on its nutritional and functional properties|journal=Food Reviews International| volume=32| pages=364–376| year=2016| last1=Serna| first1=Liliana| last2=García-Gonzales| first2=Estefanía| last3=Torres-León| first3=Cristian| issue=4| s2cid=87396909}}</ref>

==Fossil record==
The earliest [[fossil]] species thought to be related to ''Mangifera'' is ''[[Eomangiferophyllum damalgiriense]]'' from the upper [[Paleocene]] in northeastern [[India]]. Leaves have also been reported from the Paleocene of [[Japan]] and the [[Eocene]] of [[Germany]], though these have been considered questionable. Leaf fossils confidently assignable to ''Mangifera'' have been collected from [[Oligocene]] or early [[Miocene]] sediments in northern [[Thailand]].<ref>{{Cite journal |author=Prakart Sawangchote |author2=Paul J. Mango seed contains important bioactive compounds that have high [[antioxidant]] activity, lipids that have acceptable physical and chemical characteristics (free of ''trans'' fatty acids), and a somewhat high (about 6%) [[protein]] content.<ref>{{cite journal | doi=10.1016/j.tifs.2016.06.009| title=Mango seed: Functional and nutritional properties|journal=Trends in Food Science & Technology| volume=55| pages=109–117| year=2016| last1=Torres-León| first1=Cristian| last2=Rojas| first2=Romeo| last3=Serna| first3=Liliana| last4=Contreras| first4=Juan| last5=Aguilar| first5=Cristobal| s2cid=89179753}}</ref> The mango peel contains considerable amounts of [[antioxidants]] and [[dietary fiber]].<ref>{{cite journal | doi=10.1080/87559129.2015.1094815| title=Agro-industrial potential of the mango peel based on its nutritional and functional properties|journal=Food Reviews International| volume=32| pages=364–376| year=2016| last1=Serna| first1=Liliana| last2=García-Gonzales| first2=Estefanía| last3=Torres-León| first3=Cristian| issue=4| s2cid=87396909}}</ref>

==Fossil record==
The earliest [[fossil]] species thought to be related to ''Mangifera'' is ''[[Eomangiferophyllum damalgiriense]]'' from the upper [[Paleocene]] in northeastern [[India]]. Leaves have also been reported from the Paleocene of [[Japan]] and the [[Eocene]] of [[Germany]], though these have been considered questionable. Leaf fossils confidently assignable to ''Mangifera'' have been collected from [[Oligocene]] or early [[Miocene]] sediments in northern [[Thailand]].<ref>{{Cite journal |author=Prakart Sawangchote |author2=Paul J.
